patient_information: A 14-year-old boy from rural Tanzania. His history is otherwise unremarkable.
chief_complaint: Difficulty in walking for over two years.
history_of_present_illness: The patient had been well until just over two years prior to presentation, when his illness started suddenly. While walking home from school, he noticed his legs began to feel heavy and started to tremble, causing difficulty walking and a tendency to fall over. Since that day, he has been unable to stand or walk unaided. He now stands on his toes and drags his legs around with the aid of a stick. He denies any history of fever, pain, sensory, bladder or bowel symptoms. The condition has been non-progressive since its acute onset.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient lives in a village in a rural area of northern Tanzania where the main staple food crop is cassava. His diet for the two months before the illness was almost exclusively cassava. He has three siblings, one of whom is similarly affected, while their parents are fine. Identical cases had occurred in his own and neighbouring villages at around the same time.
physical_exam: The patient is well nourished and the general examination is unremarkable. Neurological examination shows he is fully orientated with normal higher mental function and cranial nerves, although bilateral optic pallor was noted on fundoscopy. His limbs reveal signs of spastic paraparesis with flexion contractures at both ankles and knees. Power in the legs is graded 3 to 4 out of 5, with greatest involvement of the knee extensors and foot dorsiflexors. There is bilateral hypertonia, hyperreflexia, and sustained ankle clonus with extensor plantar responses. His arms are normal apart from generalized hyperreflexia. There is no impairment or loss of sensation. A lumbar lordosis with thoracic kyphoscoliosis is noticeable on standing.
labs_and_diagnostics: Full blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, blood glucose, and creatinine were normal. Urine analysis was normal. Microscopy of urine and stool specimens did not show any ova of Schistosoma species. HIV serology and VDRL were negative. A lumbar puncture was normal. Radiographs of the chest and thoracolumbar spine were also normal.
differential_diagnosis: The main differential diagnosis for spastic paraparesis in this setting includes spinal tuberculosis (Pott’s disease), transverse myelitis, spinal cord infections like schistosomiasis, and spinal malignancy. However, these were considered very unlikely due to the isolated motor involvement without sensory or bladder symptoms, the absence of back pain, and the acute, non-progressive course. The strong epidemiological link to an almost exclusive cassava diet and other similar cases in the community pointed towards a tropical nutritional myeloneuropathy, with the final clinical diagnosis being konzo.
management_and_clinical_course: There is no cure for the patient's condition; management is supportive and aimed at symptomatic improvement and disease prevention. He uses a stick to walk. Muscle relaxants were noted to have a limited role. Surgical treatment, such as Achilles tendon lengthening, was considered but the patient was not referred due to a lack of resources and the large number of similar cases in the community. At follow-up examinations at 6 and 12 months, his condition of permanent spastic paraparesis was unchanged. He uses one stick with very restricted mobility.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis is konzo, a distinct form of tropical spastic paraparesis. This is based on the clinical criteria of an abrupt onset of a permanent, non-progressive, symmetrical spastic paraparesis without sensory or genitourinary involvement. The diagnosis is strongly supported by the epidemiological context: occurring in a cassava-growing area of Africa, with an overreliance on insufficiently processed cassava as a staple food for two months, and the concurrent emergence of identical cases in his sibling and community. Investigations ruled out other causes such as infections (HIV, VDRL, schistosomiasis), and structural spinal cord lesions.
